amc12-2002-12a-04.title: Set up an equation
amc12-2002-12a-04.body:
Let the angle be $x^\circ$. Its complement is $90-x$ and its supplement is $180-x$:
$$90-x=\tfrac14(180-x)\implies360-4x=180-x\implies x=60.$$

**Answer: (B) 60**

amc12-2002-12a-04.title: Supplement minus complement
amc12-2002-12a-04.body:
The supplement is always $90^\circ$ more than the complement. If the complement is $c$, the supplement is $4c$, so $3c=90$, $c=30$, and the angle is $90-30=60$.

**Answer: (B) 60**

amc12-2002-12a-13.title: Solve both cases
amc12-2002-12a-13.body:
For positive $x$, $\left|x-\frac1x\right|=1$ means $x-\frac1x=1$ or $x-\frac1x=-1$.

- $x^2-x-1=0$: positive root $\frac{1+\sqrt5}2$.
- $x^2+x-1=0$: positive root $\frac{-1+\sqrt5}2$.

These are the two different numbers, and $a+b=\frac{1+\sqrt5}2+\frac{-1+\sqrt5}2=\sqrt5$.

**Answer: (C) $\sqrt5$**

amc12-2002-12a-13.title: Reciprocal pair
amc12-2002-12a-13.body:
If $a-\frac1a=1$, then $b=\frac1a$ satisfies $b-\frac1b=-1$, so the two numbers are reciprocals: $ab=1$ and $a-b=1$. Then $(a+b)^2=(a-b)^2+4ab=1+4=5$, so $a+b=\sqrt5$.

**Answer: (C) $\sqrt5$**

amc12-2002-12a-17.title: Even digits must be in the tens place
amc12-2002-12a-17.body:
A prime with two or more digits can't end in $4$, $6$ or $8$ (even), so these digits must sit in the tens place or higher, contributing at least $10(4+6+8)=180$. The other digits $1,2,3,5,7,9$ contribute at least their face value, $27$. So the sum is at least $207$.

It's achievable: $\{2,3,5,41,67,89\}$ uses each digit once, all are prime, and $2+3+5+41+67+89=207$.

**Answer: (B) 207**

amc12-2002-12a-18.title: Internal tangent
amc12-2002-12a-18.body:
$C_1$ has center $A=(10,0)$, radius $6$; $C_2$ has center $B=(-15,0)$, radius $9$; $AB=25$. The circles are separate, so there are external and internal common tangents.

For an internal tangent (crossing between the circles) at points $P,Q$, it meets $AB$ at $D$ with $\triangle APD\sim\triangle BQD$ (right angles at $P,Q$) in ratio $6:9$, so $AD=10$, $BD=15$. Then $PD=\sqrt{10^2-6^2}=8$ and $QD=\sqrt{15^2-9^2}=12$: $PQ=20$.

An external tangent has length $\sqrt{25^2-(9-6)^2}=\sqrt{616}\approx24.8$, longer. So the shortest is $20$.

**Answer: (C) 20**

amc12-2002-12a-18.title: Formula
amc12-2002-12a-18.body:
For circles with radii $r_1,r_2$ and center distance $d$, the internal tangent segment has length $\sqrt{d^2-(r_1+r_2)^2}=\sqrt{625-225}=20$, shorter than the external one $\sqrt{d^2-(r_1-r_2)^2}$.

**Answer: (C) 20**

amc12-2002-12a-19.title: Work from the outside in
amc12-2002-12a-19.body:
First, $f(y)=6$ exactly at $y=-2$ and $y=1$ (the two peaks). So we need $f(x)=-2$ or $f(x)=1$.

- $f(x)=-2$: the line $y=-2$ meets the graph on the left segment (rising from $-4$ to $6$) and on the right segment (falling from $6$ to $-6$). The middle part is $\ge0$. **2 solutions.**
- $f(x)=1$: the line $y=1$ meets each of the four segments once (each spans from below $1$ to $6$ or vice versa). **4 solutions.**

Total: $6$.

**Answer: (D) 6**

amc12-2002-12a-20.title: Divisors of 99
amc12-2002-12a-20.body:
$0.\overline{ab}=\frac{\overline{ab}}{99}$, so in lowest terms the denominator divides $99=3^2\cdot11$, and it isn't $1$ (since $\overline{ab}\ne0,99$). The candidates are $3,9,11,33,99$, and all occur:
$\frac{33}{99}=\frac13$, $\frac{11}{99}=\frac19$, $\frac{9}{99}=\frac1{11}$, $\frac{3}{99}=\frac1{33}$, $\frac1{99}$.

That's $5$ denominators.

**Answer: (C) 5**

amc12-2002-12a-21.title: Find the period
amc12-2002-12a-21.body:
Continue the sequence: $4,7,1,8,9,7,6,3,9,2,1,3,4,7,\dots$ It repeats every $12$ terms (since $4,7$ reappears), and one period sums to $60$.

$166$ periods give $1992$ terms with sum $9960$. We need more than $40$ more: the running sums of $4,7,1,8,9,7,6$ are $4,11,12,20,29,36,42$, so $7$ more terms are needed. $n=1992+7=1999$.

**Answer: (B) 1999**

amc12-2002-12a-22.title: Find where D must be
amc12-2002-12a-22.body:
Since $\angle B=60^\circ$ and $AB=10$: $BC=5$ and $AC=5\sqrt3$. As $D$ moves along $AC$, $BD^2=BC^2+CD^2=25+CD^2$, so $BD>5\sqrt2\iff CD>5$.

Let $D_0$ be the point on $AC$ with $CD_0=5$. The condition holds exactly when $P$ lies in triangle $BD_0A$. Triangles $BD_0A$ and $BCA$ share the height $BC$, so the probability is
$$\frac{D_0A}{CA}=\frac{5\sqrt3-5}{5\sqrt3}=\frac{3-\sqrt3}{3}.$$

**Answer: (C) $\frac{3-\sqrt3}{3}$**

amc12-2002-12a-23.title: Similar triangles
amc12-2002-12a-23.body:
$D$ is on the perpendicular bisector of $BC$, so $DB=DC=7$ and $\angle DBC=\angle C$. Since $BD$ bisects $\angle B$, also $\angle ABD=\angle C$.

So triangles $ABD$ and $ACB$ share $\angle A$ and have $\angle ABD=\angle ACB$: they are similar, giving $\frac{AB}{AC}=\frac{AD}{AB}$, i.e. $AB^2=AD\cdot AC=9\cdot16=144$, $AB=12$.

Triangle $ABD$ has sides $12,9,7$. By Heron's formula with $s=14$:
$$[ABD]=\sqrt{14\cdot2\cdot5\cdot7}=\sqrt{980}=14\sqrt5.$$

**Answer: (D) $14\sqrt5$**

amc12-2002-12a-23.title: Isosceles height
amc12-2002-12a-23.body:
As above, $AB=12$. Instead of Heron, drop the altitude from $B$ to line $AD$ in triangle $ABD$ ($AB=12$, $BD=7$, $AD=9$). If its foot is at signed distance $u$ from $A$ along $AD$, then $144-u^2=49-(9-u)^2$, so $18u=176$, $u=\frac{88}9$, and the height is $\sqrt{144-\frac{7744}{81}}=\frac{\sqrt{3920}}9=\frac{28\sqrt5}9$. Area $=\frac12\cdot9\cdot\frac{28\sqrt5}9=14\sqrt5$.

**Answer: (D) $14\sqrt5$**

amc12-2002-12a-24.title: Modulus, then roots of unity
amc12-2002-12a-24.body:
Let $z=a+bi$; the equation is $z^{2002}=\bar z$. Taking absolute values, $|z|^{2002}=|z|$, so $|z|=0$ or $|z|=1$.

- $|z|=0$: $z=0$ works ($1$ solution).
- $|z|=1$: then $\bar z=\frac1z$, so the equation becomes $z^{2003}=1$, which has $2003$ distinct solutions, all with $|z|=1$.

Total: $2004$ ordered pairs.

**Answer: (E) 2004**

amc12-2002-12a-24.title: Polar form
amc12-2002-12a-24.body:
For $z\ne0$ write $z=re^{i\theta}$: $r^{2002}e^{2002i\theta}=re^{-i\theta}$, so $r=1$ and $2003\theta\equiv0\pmod{2\pi}$, i.e. $\theta=\frac{2\pi k}{2003}$, $k=0,\dots,2002$: $2003$ solutions. Adding $z=0$ gives $2004$.

**Answer: (E) 2004**

amc12-2002-12a-25.title: Evaluate at x = 1
amc12-2002-12a-25.body:
Suppose $P$ has $k$ nonzero coefficients with mean $m$. Then $P(1)$ is the sum of its coefficients, $km$, and $Q(1)$ is the sum of $k$ copies of $m$, also $km$. So $P(1)=Q(1)$: the two graphs must meet at $x=1$.

Among the pictures, only (B) shows the two curves crossing at $x=1$. (For instance $P(x)=2x^4-3x^2-3x-4$ has mean coefficient $-2$, giving $Q(x)=-2x^4-2x^2-2x-2$, and $P(1)=Q(1)=-8$.)

**Answer: (B)**
